Synergistic promotion of straw anaerobic digestion by a composite 
microbial consortium and micro-aeration: Enhancing lignocellulose 
decomposition and methanogenesis
Junyi Zheng , Xuepeng Wang , Yaobin Zhang *
a Dalian University of Technology, School of Environmental Science and Technology, No. 2 Linggong Road, Ganjingzi District. Dalian, Liaoning, 116024, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Reactive oxygen species
Intermittent micro-aeration
Composite microbial consortium
Anaerobic digestion
A B S T R A C T
The stable structure of lignocellulose is the main obstacle to the anaerobic digestion of agricultural straw. In this 
study, a composite microbial consortium composed of Phanerochaete chrysosporium and Aspergillus niger, coupled 
with intermittent micro-aeration, was employed to enhance lignocellulose decomposition and methanogenesis. 
Under an optimal micro-aeration intensity of 4 % (Vair:Vreactor/day), methane production was 22.57 % higher 
than that under strict anaerobic conditions. A higher aeration intensity (6 %) further improved organic matter 
removal, but decreased methane production. Micro-aeration induced periodic fluctuations in oxidation-reduction 
potential during anaerobic digestion to form reactive oxygen species, which significantly enhanced the activities 
of lignin peroxidase (2.92-fold), manganese peroxidase (1.99-fold), and laccase (2.83-fold), thereby accelerating 
lignin decomposition and humus formation. The resulting humic substances acted as natural electron shuttles, 
facilitating microbial electron transfer and elevating intracellular NADH/NAD+ ratios, which ultimately stimu­
lated methanogenesis. Microbial community analysis confirmed that the inoculated fungi survived and remained 
metabolically active under micro-aerobic conditions, effectively degrading lignocellulose to provide accessible 
substrates for methanogens. This study demonstrated that integrating a composite fungal consortium with 
controlled micro-aeration could be a robust and efficient strategy for valorizing straw waste.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion is an efficient approach for agricultural waste 
management by converting organic solids into methane or valuable 
chemicals such as fatty acids. However, agricultural residues like crop 
straw mainly consist of lignocellulose—a complex and chemically stable 
mixture of lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose—which resists microbial 
breakdown and thus limits the digestion efficiency [1,2]. Phanerochaete 
chrysosporium, an aerobic lignin-decomposing fungus, secretes extra­
cellular enzymes such as lignin peroxidase (LiP), manganese peroxidase 
(MnP), and laccase (Lac) to decompose lignin [3]. Specifically, oxidases 
and dismutases in P. chrysosporium catalyze oxygen reductions: first, O2 
accepts two electrons to form superoxide anions (•O2
−; O2 + 2e−→ •O2
−), 
which then disproportionate in the presence of protons to generate 
hydrogen peroxide (2•O2
−+ 2H+ → H2O2 + O2). This initiates Fenton- 
like reactions (Fe2+ + H2O2 → Fe3+ + •OH + OH−) [4], where hy­
droxyl radicals (•OH) cleave aromatic structures and β-O-4 ether bonds 
in lignin, disrupting its protective matrix and improving the accessibility 
of cellulose for enzymatic hydrolysis [5–7]. Additionally, phenolic 
compounds derived from lignin decomposition undergo enzyme- 
catalyzed polymerization and humification [8,9]. Owing to these 
properties, Phanerochaete chrysosporium has been widely applied in 
aerobic composting and anaerobic pretreatment processes [10,11].
Methanogenesis requires strict anaerobic conditions. However, 
recent research has demonstrated that controlled micro-aeration in 
anaerobic digestion systems can promote the enrichment of hydrolytic 
and acidogenic microorganisms (including actinomycetes and fungi) 
without inhibiting methanogens [12–14]. Notably, Gong et al. recently 
reported that Phanerochaete chrysosporium secreted ligninolytic enzymes 
under intermittent micro-aeration, thereby accelerating straw decom­
position and enhancing digestion efficiency [15].
While Phanerochaete chrysosporium primarily targets lignin decom­
position, its effectiveness on cellulose and hemicellulose is limited. 
Aspergillus niger, however, is capable of breaking cellulose into

cellobiose, which may be converted into glucose via β-glucosidase. 
Additionally, Aspergillus niger secretes various hydrolytic enzymes that 
decompose hemicellulose's complex backbone and side chains, releasing 
monosaccharides like xylo-oligosaccharides [16–18]. Therefore, a 
composite microbial consortium composed of Phanerochaete chrys­
osporium and Aspergillus niger is hypothesized to achieve synergistic 
decomposition of straw lignocellulose. Notably, composite fungi have 
been widely used in aerobic composting, but there are few studies on 
their direct application in anaerobic digestion [19].Additionally, 
controlled micro-aeration is known to improve lignocellulose decom­
position by facilitating the activity of oxidative enzymes and promoting 
the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) [20]. Intermittent 
micro-aeration has been previously reported to minimize the inhibitory 
effects of excessive oxygen on strictly anaerobic methanogens while 
enhancing lignocellulose decomposition [12,21]. Therefore, it is 
assumed that integrating a composite microbial consortium with opti­
mized intermittent micro-aerobic conditions might further enhance 
straw decomposition and methane production. So far, no reports have 
been found on the application of composite fungi combined with micro- 
aeration in anaerobic digestion.
Consequently, this study employed a composite microbial con­
sortium of Phanerochaete chrysosporium and Aspergillus niger, combined 
with intermittent micro-aeration, to enhance lignocellulose decompo­
sition and methanogenesis. The objectives were to evaluate the feasi­
bility of this combined strategy and to elucidate the underlying 
mechanisms. Specifically, this study investigated how hydroxyl radicals 
(•OH) disrupt lignocellulosic structures to enhance anaerobic biode­
gradability. Additionally, the impact of micro-aeration on microbial 
community was explored. This study was expected to provide a prom­
ising strategy to enhance the anaerobic digestion of agricultural waste.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Experimental materials
The inoculated sludge used in the anaerobic digestion experiments, 
the sludge from a wastewater treatment plant in Dalian, was stored 
anaerobically at 4 ◦C in the laboratory. Its chemical oxygen demand 
(COD), 48770 ± 413 mg/L. Corn straw was purchased from a farm 
(Lianyungang, China), chopped, ground into powder, and screened to a 
particle size of approximately 0.15 mm and used as the sole digestion 
substrate, without any additional carbon sources. The basic character­
istics of the corn straw and the sludge are presented in Table S1. The 
mixed sludge was activated for 5 days prior to straw addition. Phaner­
ochaete chrysosporium and Aspergillus niger were obtained from Beina Bio, 
Henan Industrial Microbial Strain Engineering Research Center. The 
fungi were activated on potato dextrose agar (PDA) and incubated at 
30 ◦C for 5 days. Colonies were scraped and rinsed with sterile water to 
obtain spore suspensions. The suspensions were diluted to 2 × 108 
spores/mL based on plate count results (colony-forming units, CFU) and 
stored at −80 ◦C for subsequent use.
2.2. Experimental design
The anaerobic digestion of corn straw was conducted in batch modes. 
Each reactor had an effective working volume of 200 mL (inner diam­
eter: 60 mm; height: 70 mm), which was equipped with two sampling 
ports at the top for feeding or discharge, and biogas collection. A 500 mL 
gas sampling bag was connected for biogas collection. Batch tests were 
first conducted to evaluate the effects of microbial consortium and 
micro-aeration on biogas production. Each reactor was filled with 100 
mL of mixed sludge (see Section 2.1), 20 mL of spore suspension (10mL 
per strain), and 80 mL of distilled water. Each reactor received 6 g of dry 
corn straw. The ratio of sludge to spore suspension (100 mL:20 mL) was 
determined based on preliminary batch tests (data not shown) aimed at 
optimizing fungal activity without causing system acidification or 
instability.
The experiments were divided into three groups: the control group 
(no microbial inoculum, anaerobic conditions), the anaerobic inocula­
tion group, and the micro-aerobic inoculation group with air volumes of 
5 mL (air volume ratio [Vair/Vreactor] = 2 %). Subsequently, the effects of 
aeration intensity on methane production were evaluated under com­
parable conditions: each reactor was loaded with 100 mL of mixed 
sludge, 20 mL of spore suspension (10mL per strain), and 80 mL of 
distilled water. Every 3 days, 10 mL of substrate (containing 2 g of 
straw) was fed and an equal volume of digestate was discharged to 
maintain a hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 60 days. Four aeration 
groups were tested, with air volumes of 0 (control), 5, 10, and 15 mL (air 
volume ratio [Vair/Vreactor] = 0 %, 2 %, 4 %, 6 %), designated as Control, 
2 % Air, 4 % Air, and 6 % Air. Air was injected into the reactors via a 20- 
mL syringe through the feeding port, with a single injection every 24 h. 
The injection process lasted for approximately 5 s to ensure diffusion. All 
reactors were operated at 37 ◦C for 60 days.
To address questions regarding the causal link of the fungi and the 
mechanism of inhibition at aeration, supplementary batch experiments 
for mechanistic validation was conducted (see Supporting Material for 
details).
2.3. Analytical methods
Chemical oxygen demand (COD) was measured by standard 
methods. Methane production was determined by gas chromatography 
with a thermal conductivity detector (Tianmei GC-7900, China), 
equipped with a TCD and a GDX — 102/80–100 mesh packed column. 
Nitrogen was used as the carrier gas at 40 mL/min. The temperatures of 
the injector, column, and detector were set at 140 ◦C, 220 ◦C, and 
160 ◦C, respectively. The morphology of sludge and straw was examined 
using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, HITACHI SU5000, China) 
[22]. Sludge electrochemical properties (cyclic voltammetry [CV] and 
electrochemical impedance spectroscopy [EIS]) were analyzed (see 
Supporting Material). Electron accepting capacity (EAC) and electron 
donating capacity (EDC) were used to evaluate the electron accepting/ 
donating capacity of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) [23].
The activities of lignin peroxidase (LiP), manganese peroxidase 
(MnP), and laccase (Lac) were determined using enzyme-linked immu­
nosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. Cellulase activity was measured by pre­
vious methods (see Supporting Material). Lignin, cellulose, and 
hemicellulose contents were determined following the Van Soest 
method [24].
ROS were detected using EPR spectroscopy (EMXPlus, Bruker A300, 
Germany). 2,2,6,6-Tetramethylpiperidine (TEMP) and 5,5-Dimethyl-1- 
pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) were used as spin traps for •O2
−
and •OH, 
respectively. Samples were ultrasonically dispersed in water or meth­
anol, mixed with spin traps, and analyzed using capillaries in the EPR 
instrument. Superoxide anion radical (•O2
−) was quantified using the 2,3- 
bis(2-methoxy-4-nitro-5-sulfophenyl)-5-carboxypyridine 
tetrazolium 
[XTT] assay. Hydroxyl radicals (•OH) were quantitatively analyzed 
using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) by trapping 
them with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), which reacts to generate form­
aldehyde (HCHO), following the procedure outlined in Text S1.
Oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) and headspace oxygen were 
measured using an ORP electrode (Model STARTER 3100, USA) and a 
fiber optic oxygen transmitter (FiBox3, PreSens GmbH, Germany). These 
parameters, rather than dissolved oxygen (DO), were selected as they 
more accurately reflect the bulk redox conditions and the transient ox­
ygen exposure in the anaerobic headspace. Each group of 250 mL re­
actors was tested continuously for 24 h, Excitation-emission matrix 
(EEM) fluorescence spectra were obtained using an Agilent Cary Eclipse 
spectrophotometer (Santa Clara, CA, USA). Fourier-transform infrared 
spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis was conducted using a Thermo Nicolet 
IS50 spectrometer (scan range: 4000–400 cm−1, resolution: 4 cm−1).

2.4. Microbial community analysis
At the end of the experiment, sludge samples were collected for high- 
throughput 16S rRNA sequencing. Microbial DNA was extracted using a 
rapid soil DNA extraction kit. The V3–V4 regions of archaea and bac­
teria, and the ITS region of fungi were amplified by PCR. Purified PCR 
products were used to construct libraries with the Illumina TruSeq DNA 
protocol and sequenced on an Illumina TruSeq 2000 platform. The 
sequencing data have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read 
Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession number PRJNA1367766.
2.5. Statistical analysis
All experiments were conducted in triplicate, and data are presented 
as mean ± standard deviation unless otherwise noted. Statistical com­
parisons between groups were performed using one-way analysis of 
variance (ANOVA) followed by SPSS 22.0. A p-value < 0.05 was 
considered statistically significant.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Enhancement of anaerobic digestion performance
3.1.1. Effects of the microbial consortium and micro-aeration
In sequential batch anaerobic digesters using straw as the substrate, a 
microbial consortium of Phanerochaete chrysosporium and Aspergillus 
niger was integrated with micro-aeration to evaluate the performance of 
the digesters. The results clearly indicated that the benefits of the fungal 
consortium were oxygen-dependent. Under strictly anaerobic conditions 
without aeration (Fig. S1), the consortium provided negligible benefits; 
methane production in the anaerobic inoculation group (218.9 mL) was 
marginally higher than in the anaerobic control group (205.7 mL). In 
sharp contrast, under micro-aerobic conditions (2 % air), the consortium 
increased methane production to 247.3 mL, a 20.2 % increase over the 
anaerobic control group. This demonstrated that micro-aeration is 
essential to activate the metabolic functions of the inoculated fungi for 
enhancing anaerobic digestion.
3.1.2. Effect of aeration intensity
Under semi-continuous feeding with a single-dose fungal consortium 
inoculation, the effects of aeration intensity on methane production 
were investigated. Results (Fig. 1A, B) revealed that the 4 % air group 
achieved the highest methane production, which was 15.93 % higher 
than the no-air control group (17.75 vs. 15.31 mL/g VS⋅day). compared 
to the no-air control group, the 2 % and 6 % aeration groups increased 
by 13.78 % (17.42 ± 0.96 mL/g VS⋅day) and 13.12 % (17.32 ± 0.98 
mL/g VS⋅day), respectively. Cumulative methane production reached 
1392 mL (2 % air group), 1607 mL (4 % air group), and 1465 mL (6 % air 
group), which were 6.17 %, 22.57 %, and 11.75 % higher than the 
control (1311 mL), respectively. This 22.57 % enhancement must be 
benchmarked against other recent strategies for straw valorization. For 
instance, in-situ additives, such as nano-bubble technology, have re­
ported comparable gains (24.08 %) [25]. In contrast, dedicated, energy- 
intensive methods like hydrothermal pretreatment could achieve 
significantly higher yields, reaching 152.28 % [26]. However, the pri­
mary advantage of the in-situ approach lied not in achieving the abso­
lute maximum yield, but in avoiding the high capital and energy costs 
associated with a separate pretreatment step. The value of this method 
was the operational simplicity. The total chemical oxygen demand 
(tCOD) decreased in the aerated groups (Fig. 1C, D), which were 1.39 ×
106 mg/L at 2 % aeration, 1.35 × 106 mg/L at 4 % aeration, and 1.30 ×
106 mg/L at 6 % aeration. These represented reductions of 4.36 %, 7.20 
%, and 8.91 % compared with the control group (1.45 × 106 mg/L), 
respectively. Conversely, the soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD) 
levels in the aerated groups were 2341 mg/L at 2 % aeration, 2533 mg/L 
at 4 % aeration, and 2331 mg/L at 6 % aeration, all of which were higher 
than that of the control group (2255 mg/L), indicating that micro- 
aeration enhanced the hydrolysis and acidogenesis of lignocellulose to 
increase the production of soluble carbon compounds [27,28]. Collec­
tively, the results confirmed that the combination of the composite

microbial consortium and micro-aeration promoted the decomposition 
of organic matter and enhanced methane production. Although the cu­
mulative methane production had not reached a complete plateau by 
day 60 (Fig. 1A), the experiment was terminated as the daily methane 
production rates (Fig. 1B) and COD removal (Fig. 1C, D) in the semi- 
continuous reactors had reached a relatively stable state, allowing for 
a robust comparison of performance under the different aeration 
intensities.
It is noteworthy that while the 6 % air group in the semi-continuous 
run exhibited high tCOD removal, its methane production was inhibited. 
To validate the mechanism, VFA concentrations were quantified in the 
supplementary batch experiment. The results (presented in Fig. S4) 
confirmed this hypothesis: The 4 % aeration group (Fungi-MA) main­
tained a low VFA concentration [265.57–767.50 mg/L]. In contrast, the 
6 % aeration group (Fungi-MA-6 %) showed the VFA accumulation, 
reaching [313.59–888.94 mg/L], primarily composed of acetate and 
propionate.
This evidence strongly supported that excessive aeration (6 %) 
caused a “decoupling” of hydrolysis from methanogenesis, where the 
oxygen inhibited VFA-consuming methanogens, leading to VFA accu­
mulation and the observed drop in methane production.
3.2. Lignocellulose decomposition
Micro-aeration significantly enhanced lignocellulose removal 
(Fig. 2A), as evidenced by decreasing digestate residue levels in the 
following order: no air > 6 % air > 2 % air > 4 % air. The 4 % air group 
exhibited the lowest lignocellulose content (52.06 %: hemicellulose with 
15.34 %, cellulose with 29.90 %, lignin with 7.71 %). This was followed 
by the 2 % air group (53.63 %: 14.87 %, 31.11 %, 7.69 %, respectively) 
and the 6 % air group (55.05 %: 16.04 %, 30.16 %, 8.84 %, respectively). 
The control group retained the highest lignocellulose content (59.99 %: 
21.38 %, 29.92 %, 8.68 %). The lignocellulose residue in the 4 % air 
group was 7.93 percentage point lower than that in the control group. 
These results confirmed that the combination of the composite microbial 
consortium and micro-aeration enhanced lignocellulose decomposition.
Micro-aeration also increased the activity of lignocellulolytic en­
zymes. Laccase activity was highest in the 4 % air group (0.51 U/mL), 
2.83-fold higher than the control group (0.18 U/mL). Other enzymes 
peaked in the 6 % air group: lignin peroxidase (LiP, 0.18 U/mL vs. 0.06 
U/mL), manganese peroxidase (MnP, 2.76 U/mL vs. 1.39 U/mL), and 
cellobiohydrolase (0.19 U/mL vs. 0.16 U/mL). These activation levels 
are significant, as previously noted that [29].Overall, the activities of 
lignocellulose-degrading enzymes were significantly higher in the 
micro-aerated groups than in the control group (Fig. 2B–E), indicating 
that micro-aerobic conditions promoted the secretion of key oxidative 
enzymes involved in lignocellulose breakdown [30,31]. Moreover, the 
enzymatic activity exhibited a positive correlation with oxygen con­
centration, thereby accelerating the decomposition of lignocellulose and 
facilitating the release of sCOD for the subsequent methanogenesis [2].
Accordingly, morphological analysis of straw digestate (Fig. S2) 
showed that the residues of the control group was of compact structure, 
while the residues of the three aerated groups were clearly fragmented. 
Besides, the aerated groups exhibited dense fungal mycelia and 
macroscopic fungal aggregates, which was the result of the active fungal 
metabolism. The aggregates observed in the aerated groups might have 
improved microbial tolerance to oxygen stress [32].
3.3. Redox potential and ROS
Since these lignocellulolytic enzymes require oxidative triggers, it 
was hypothesized that micro-aeration induced Reactive Oxygen Species 
(ROS). Oxidation-Reduction Potential (ORP) and headspace oxygen 
concentrations were quantified (Fig. 3A). Oxygen levels increased in the 
beginning of aeration, and then declined. Higher aeration intensities 
delayed the oxygen depletion. Specifically, in 2 % air group, the head­
space oxygen concentration peaked at 2.52 % at 3.5 h and was depleted 
at 13.5 h, while in the 6 % air group, the oxygen concentration peaked at 
4.25 % at 4.5 h and took 15.5 h to deplete.

Quantification of •OH showed that aeration facilitated the •OH

The 6 % air group showed a 33.3 % increase over the 2 % group (50.96 
vs. 38.23 μmol/L). Negligible •OH was detected in the control group. 
Stronger redox oscillations at the higher aeration condition likely 
intensified Fenton-like reactions to enhance organic removal but 
inhibiting methanogenesis, consistent with the lower methane produc­
tion in 6 % air group.

3.4. Effects of micro-aeration on straw humification
The controlled introduction of air into the anaerobic digestion sys­
tem could accelerate humification. The ROS-driven enzymatic degra­
dation of lignin generated phenolic intermediates, a process driven by 
extracellular oxidative enzymes secreted by microorganisms. These en­
zymes decomposed lignin to produce phenolics and other aromatics, 
which were then polymerized into complex and stable humic substances 
[39,40]. Due to its rich aromatic structure, lignin was highly susceptible 
to enzymatic oxidation, serving as a primary substrate for the generation 
of humic substances precursors [41–43]. Under micro-aerobic condi­
tions, extracellular enzymes such as laccase (Lac), lignin peroxidase 
(LiP), and manganese peroxidase (MnP), secreted primarily by Phaner­
ochaete chrysosporium, played a central role in initiating these trans­
formations. Specifically, they attacked lignin via distinct catalytic 
pathways: Lac oxidized phenolic units to phenoxyl radicals; the high- 
redox-potential LiP directly oxidized non-phenolic rings to cation radi­
cals; and MnP utilized a diffusible Mn(III)-chelate as a redox mediator 
[44].
The highly reactive radical intermediates generated by these enzy­
matic actions could directly initiate the depolymerization and structural 
modification of lignin. It included the preferential cleavage of ether 
bonds, such as the prevalent β-O-4 linkage, and the oxidation of C-α side 
chains to form carbonyl and carboxyl groups, thereby releasing phenolic

monomers like vanillin and syringaldehyde. Concurrently, the products 
and intermediates of these enzymatic reactions (H2O2 and quinones/ 
hydroquinones) could engage in subsequent chemical reactions, such as 
quinone redox cycling and Fenton-like reactions, leading to the indirect 
generation of highly potent hydroxyl radicals (•OH). As non-selective, 
powerful oxidants, these hydroxyl radicals further attack and disrupt 
lignin, promoting aromatic ring-opening to form intermediates such as 
vanillic acid (Fig. 4A), which served as fundamental building blocks for 
subsequent humification processes.
FTIR and EEM analysis were conducted to investigate the humifi­
cation. FTIR spectra (Fig. S3; key absorption bands summarized in 
Table S2) demonstrated that freeze-dried samples from the aeration 
groups exhibited distinct structural alterations of lignocellulose after 
anaerobic digestion. Notably, the intensity of characteristic absorption

bands associated with lignocellulose decomposition was significantly 
augmented, including O–H stretching (3400–3420 cm−1), C–H vibra­
tions of methyl and methoxy groups (2980–2840 cm−1), aromatic ring 
skeletal vibrations (1690–1500 cm−1), and C–O stretching vibrations of 
aromatic ethers (1050–1000 cm−1). Additionally, the absorption band 
centered at approximately 1650 cm−1 was significantly intensified in the 
aeration groups. The band represents a composite signal attributable to 
aromatic C––C skeletal vibrations, asymmetric C––O stretching of 
carboxylate groups (COO−), and C––O stretching in quinone structures 
[45]. The increased intensity provided strong evidence of oxidative 
transformation catalyzed by enzymes like laccase, leading to an increase 
in the aromaticity and the relative content of oxygen-containing func­
tional groups, particularly quinone-like structures.
Further evidence was provided by EEM fluorescence analysis 
(Fig. 5B–E). Compared to the control group, the samples from the 
aeration groups exhibited higher fluorescence intensity in the charac­
teristic regions for humic- and fulvic-like substances (Excitation/Emis­
sion: 250–400 nm/380–500 nm) [46]. The fluorescence enhancement 
indicated a significant increase in the content or structural complexity of 
fluorescent dissolved organic matter components. This finding was 
consistent with the FTIR observations of lignocellulose decomposition 
and aromatic restructuring, demonstrating that micro-aerobic condi­
tions promoted the degree of humification.
Collectively, these findings indicated that the aeration fostered the 
enzymatic and radical-driven humification processes, significantly 
enhancing the conversion of straw lignin into humic substances during 
anaerobic digestion. The enhanced humification process promoted 
organic waste stabilization and concurrently stimulated microbial 
metabolic activity, thereby improving the efficiency of the digestion 
system.
3.5. Electrochemical analysis
The enhanced humification carried a significance in anaerobic sys­
tems that was often overlooked. To further explore potential mecha­
nisms that promoted methane production, electrochemical properties of 
sludge and the role of humic substances were assessed. Cyclic voltam­
metry (CV) analysis (Fig. 6A) revealed significantly increased sludge 
capacitance under micro-aerobic conditions (2 % air: 1.187 × 10−3 F; 4 
% air: 1.280 × 10−3 F; 6 % air: 1.203 × 10−3 F), representing im­
provements of 8.01 %, 16.47 %, and 9.46 % relative to the control group 
(1.099 × 10−3 F). The augmented capacitance indicated the enhance­
ment of charge storage capability and the improvement of conductivity 
within the sludge matrix, which was beneficial for facilitating microbial 
electron transfer [47]. Correspondingly, electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy (EIS) showed that the resistance of digestate samples in 
aeration groups (Fig. 6B) was 18.42 %–29.23 % lower than the control 
group, indicating the lower resistance of the sludge after the micro- 
aeration [48].
Humic substances, rich in quinone functional groups, are known to 
play a critical role as electron shuttles within microbial ecosystems, 
likely accelerating interspecies electron transfer and thereby enhancing 
anaerobic metabolisms. In this study, micro-aeration stimulated the

Electron donating capacity (EAC) and electron donating capacity 
(EDC) were measured in EPS extracted from the digested sludge 
(Fig. 6C). Compared to the control group (EAC: 0.90 mmol e−/g; EDC: 
0.322 mmol e−/g), the EAC values increased by 68.9 %, 52.2 %, and 
26.7 %, respectively, and the EDC values increased by 22.1 %, 37.5 %, 
and 10.2 % for the 2 %, 4 %, and 6 % air groups, respectively. The 
elevated EAC indicated the higher humification level [49], while the 
increased EDC was closely associated with the higher phenolic content 
[50]. Thus, the rise in both EAC and EDC in the aerated groups provided 
additional evidence of enhanced lignocellulose decomposition, gener­
ating a higher abundance of phenolic and aromatic intermediates. The 
humification process under micro-aerobic conditions was likely similar 
to that of aerobic composting [51], where aromatic monomers were 
polymerized into complex humic structures with oxidation processes. 
While the enhanced electrochemical properties and elevated EAC/EDC 
values strongly suggested humic substances acted as electron shuttles to 
facilitate methanogenesis, it was important to acknowledge their dual 
role. Humic substances (particularly quinone moieties) could also serve 
as terminal electron acceptors, potentially competing with methanogens 
for electrons. In this system, the 22.57 % increase in methane production 
indicated that the positive effect of humic substances as electron shuttles 
significantly outweighed any potential negative competition, ultimately 
stimulating methanogenesis. Accordingly, three-dimensional (3D) fluo­
rescence spectroscopy (Fig. 5) revealed a significantly higher charac­
teristic fluorescence intensity in aerated samples than in the control 
group. Moreover, the elevated intracellular NADH/NAD+ ratio (0.19 vs. 
0.16; Fig. 6D) indicated the enhancement of redox status and electron 
flux, thereby promoting microbial metabolic activity [22]. Overall, 
electrochemical, biochemical, and spectroscopic analysis demonstrated 
that micro-aeration facilitated humification and microbial electron 
transfer, leading to the higher methane production in anaerobic diges­
tion systems.
3.6. Validation of the fungal role and microbial dynamics
Microbial community analysis revealed that the combination of 
fungal augmentation and micro-aeration was critical for enhancing 
lignocellulose decomposition, which subsequently triggered a profound 
restructuring of the native anaerobic food chain (Fig. 7). Under micro- 
aerobic conditions, the introduced fungal strains proliferated success­
fully. Phanerochaete chrysosporium increased from a relative abundance 
of 4.40 % in the control group to 4.57–6.76 % in the aeration groups, 
while Aspergillus niger increased from 9.45 % to 9.91–28.64 %. Extra­
cellular peroxidases secreted by these fungi are known to catalyze the 
oxidative cleavage of recalcitrant lignocellulose [52], thereby increasing 
substrate bioavailability for the downstream anaerobic consortia.
A primary question regarding the fungal bio-augmentation was how 
the inoculated strains could drive systemic enhancements given their 
relatively low abundance (Fig. 7C). It was hypothesized that they act as 
specialized catalysts. To provide a direct causal link, the results from the 
supplementary batch experiment were analyzed (Fig. S5). The results 
provided unequivocal proof of the fungal synergistic role. Specifically, 
the Control-MA group (4 % air, no fungi) produced low levels of lig­
ninolytic enzymes (Laccase at 0.25 U/L). In sharp contrast, the Fungi- 
MA group (4 % air + fungi) produced higher levels (Laccase at 0.51 
U/L). Similarly, a stronger •OH radical signal was detected in the Fungi- 
MA group, while the Control-MA group showed negligible ROS 
generation.
It confirmed that the observed enhancement was not an artifact of 
micro-aeration itself, but a unique metabolic consequence of the inoc­
ulated fungal consortium being activated by micro-aeration. This vali­
dated their role as highly active, specialized “catalysts”, whose 
functional impact far outweighs their relative abundance.
Notably, the impact on the indigenous microbial community was 
multifaceted, reflecting a complex interplay of competitive and 
compensatory metabolic pathways. Key taxa in conventional methano­
genic routes were adversely affected: Methanothrix, the dominant ace­
toclastic methanogen, exhibited a reduction from 54.47 % in the control 
group to 45.39 % under 4 % aeration. Similarly, the fermentative genus 
DMER64, related to interspecies hydrogen transfer (IHT) [53], exhibited 
a dose-dependent decrease with the increase of aeration intensity, sug­
gesting that micro-aeration was unbeneficial for acetoclastic and 
hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis.
Conversely, this inhibitory effect was offset by the enrichment of taxa 
involved in rate-limiting hydrolysis and alternative methanogenic 
pathway. The archaeal genus Norank_Bathyarchaeia, known to mediate 
hemicellulose and cellulose decomposition, increased from 15.49 % to 
23.86 % under aeration, which could accelerate the breakdown of 
lignocellulosic substrates [54]. Additionally, Penicillium is a typical 
aerobic lignocellulolytic fungus, exhibited an increase from 1.40 % in 
the control group to1.51 % under 4 % aeration [55]. Furthermore, the 
enrichment of Wallemia, a genus possessing antioxidant mechanisms 
[56], likely enhanced the system's overall tolerance to oxygen.
These shifts suggested that oxygen may modulate the metabolism of 
the composite microbial consortium in anaerobic environments: while 
temporarily inhibiting canonical methanogenic pathways, it promoted 
lignocellulose degradation through the enrichment of hydrolytic taxa, 
potentially creating a metabolic balance that enhance overall methane 
production.
4. Implications
This study demonstrated that integrating Phanerochaete chrys­
osporium and Aspergillus niger with controlled micro-aeration (4 % Vair/ 
Vreactor/day) created a synergistic system for agricultural waste valori­
zation. This strategy created transient oxidative niches sufficient to 
activate the fungal ROS/enzyme pathway to break the lignin barrier 
without causing systemic failure of the methanogenic community. The 
more significant mechanistic breakthrough lied in the downstream ef­
fect. In this paradigm, waste lignin is valorized into a natural mediator 
that facilitated electron transfer, creating a powerful synergy.
From the perspective of environmental engineering, this finding had 
profound implications. It presented a practical and effective strategy to 
enhance the efficiency and throughput of existing anaerobic digestion 
facilities that handle agricultural waste. By unlocking the energy po­
tential of previously recalcitrant biomass, this method promoted the 
valorization of agricultural residues. Specifically, it increased the yields 
of renewable energy in the form of biogas and contributed to a more 
robust circular bioeconomy. For instance, in agricultural regions with 
abundant waste such as crop straw, applying this method could effec­
tively convert the waste into valuable biogas energy, reducing the 
environmental burden of waste disposal and at the same time providing 
a clean energy source.
5. Conclusion
This study demonstrated that a microbial consortium (Phanerochaete 
chrysosporium and Aspergillus niger) combined with intermittent micro- 
aeration (optimally 4 % Vair:Vreactor) enhanced methane production 
from straw by 22.57 %. The mechanism involved micro-aeration 
inducing ORP fluctuations and •OH generation. This activated the con­
sortium to secrete key lignocellulolytic enzymes (LiP, MnP, Lac), 
accelerating lignin cleavage and promoting humification. The resulting 
humic substances acted as electron shuttles, enhancing system electro­
activity and stimulating methanogenesis. Microbial analysis confirmed 
the survival of the inoculated fungi, which, despite low relative abun­
dance, acted as key catalysts for lignocellulose degradation. This study 
provided novel insights for efficient micro-aerobic digestion engineering 
of agricultural wastes.
